title: Virtual Address Spaces
summary: Every address a program uses is **virtual**: the processor translates it, page by page, into a physical location in RAM using **page tables** the operating system maintains for each process. This lesson explains the translation, the size and shape of a 64-bit address space, why some addresses are impossible, and what happens when a page is not in RAM at all.
markdown:
## Every address is translated Lesson 1.06 said each process has a private address space. Here is how that works. Every time the CPU reads or writes memory, the address goes through the **memory management unit** (MMU), part of the processor, which translates it from a **virtual address** to a **physical address**: a real location in the RAM chips. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["CPU wants
virtual 0x00007FF6A1234567"] --> M["MMU
looks up the page tables
of the current process"] M --> R["Physical 0x00000002_4C8F1567
in RAM"] ``` Translation happens in units of **pages**, 4,096 bytes (`0x1000`) each. An address splits into two parts: ``` virtual address 0x00007FF6A1234567 └────────┬───────┘└┬┘ page number offset within the page: 0x567 0x7FF6A1234 ``` The page number is looked up and replaced with a **physical frame number**; the offset stays the same. So within a page, bytes keep their order, but two neighbouring virtual pages can be anywhere in physical memory, in any order. Because each process has its own page tables, the same virtual page number leads to different frames in different processes. When the scheduler switches to another process, it switches the CPU to that process's tables (by loading the register `CR3`), and the whole address space changes in one step. ## Four levels of tables A 64-bit address space is enormous. A single flat table with one entry per page would be gigabytes per process. So the tables are a **tree** with four levels, and only the parts that are actually used exist. On x64, the 48 significant bits of an address split like this: ``` 47 39 38 30 29 21 20 12 11 0 ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬────────────┐ │ level 4 │ level 3 │ level 2 │ level 1 │ offset │ │ 9 bits │ 9 bits │ 9 bits │ 9 bits │ 12 bits │ └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴────────────┘ ``` Each 9-bit index picks one of 512 entries in a table; each entry points to the next level's table; the last level gives the physical frame. The practice task splits addresses this way. Walking four tables for every memory access would be slow, so the CPU caches recent translations in the **TLB** (translation lookaside buffer). Nearly all accesses hit the TLB and cost nothing extra. Code that jumps randomly across a very large amount of memory misses it, which is another reason (besides the cache, lesson 2.07) to keep data compact. ## The shape of a 64-bit address space x64 processors use 48 bits of address today, not 64. The top 16 bits must all copy bit 47, which splits the space into two halves with a huge gap between them: | Range | Size | Used by | |---|---|---| | `0x00000000'00000000` to `0x00007FFF'FFFFFFFF` | 128 TB | **User mode**: your process | | (the gap) | | Not valid: using an address here is an immediate fault | | `0xFFFF8000'00000000` to `0xFFFFFFFF'FFFFFFFF` | 128 TB | **Kernel mode**: shared by all processes, inaccessible from user mode | Addresses in the valid ranges are called **canonical**. That is why every user-mode pointer you print starts with `0000`, and why the top two bytes in the Memory window are always `00 00` (lesson 2.11). A pointer like `0x12345678'9ABCDEF0` is not just invalid, it is impossible, and is a sure sign of corrupted data. Within the user half, Windows places the program's modules near the top (`0x00007FF...`), and stacks and heaps lower down, at addresses randomised each run (lesson 6.09). The first 64 KB (`0x0` to `0xFFFF`) are never mapped, so that a null pointer plus a small offset always faults. ## Pages that are not in RAM A page table entry can also say **"not present"**. Touching such a page raises a **page fault**, an exception the kernel handles: | Why it was not present | What the kernel does | |---|---| | The page was never committed (lesson 6.03), or is in the gap | The access is invalid: the program gets an **access violation** | | It was committed but never touched yet | Finds a free frame, fills it with zeros, maps it, and resumes the program: a **demand-zero** fault | | It was moved out to the page file on disk to free RAM | Reads it back, maps it, resumes: a **hard** fault, which takes milliseconds | | It is part of a file mapping (the `.exe`'s code, a DLL) | Reads it from the file, maps it, resumes | The program never notices the middle three, except as a pause. This is how a 100 GB address space can exist on a PC with 16 GB of RAM, and why a game that uses more memory than the machine has starts to stutter: its pages are going to and from disk. Task Manager's **Commit size** and **Working set** columns show how much memory a process has committed and how much is currently in RAM. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Thinking a pointer value is a RAM location > It is virtual. The physical location may change and is never visible to user-mode code. > [!warning] Ignoring a non-canonical pointer in a crash > A pointer with random high bits is corrupted data: look for whatever overwrote it, not for the code that used it. > [!warning] Assuming memory use is the same as RAM use > Committed memory may be in the page file; RAM in use is the working set. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? How many bytes is a page on x64 Windows, and how many bits of an address are the offset within it? - 1,024 bytes; the low 10 bits + 4,096 bytes; the low 12 bits - 65,536 bytes; the low 16 bits - 4,096 bytes; the low 16 bits > 2 to the power of 12 is 4,096, so 12 bits are needed to pick a byte within a page. 64 KB is the allocation granularity, not the page size. ? What is a canonical address? + One whose bits 48 to 63 all copy bit 47 - Any address that is a multiple of the page size - An address that has been translated to a physical address - The preferred load address written in an `.exe` > Only canonical addresses are valid, which is why user-mode pointers on x64 start with `0000`. User-mode addresses are in the lower half, kernel ones in the upper half. ? What happens when a program touches a page that was paged out to disk? - The program crashes with an access violation - The operating system restarts the program + A page fault: the kernel reads it back and resumes the program - The CPU reads the value directly from the disk > The program only notices a delay; to it the memory was always there. ? What does the MMU replace when it translates an address? - The whole address, with a random one + The page number, with a physical frame number - Only the offset within the page > Translation works page by page. ? Why does every user-mode pointer on x64 Windows start with `0000`? - Windows wastes the first two bytes - Pointers are padded for alignment + User addresses are low, so the top 16 bits are zero > Canonical user-mode addresses have bits 48 to 63 equal to bit 47, which is 0. ? What is a demand-zero page fault? + A first touch of committed memory, given a zeroed page - A crash caused by a null pointer - A page that was written to disk > It is invisible to the program, apart from a tiny delay. ? Why are page tables a tree rather than one flat array? - Because the CPU cannot read arrays + So only the parts of the address space in use need tables - To make translation faster than a flat table > A flat table for 48-bit addresses would need billions of entries per process. ```
ideas:
- Print the address of a local, a global and a heap block, and split each into page number and offset by hand.
- Open Task Manager's Details tab and add the **Commit size** and **Working set (memory)** columns. Compare them for a game or a browser.
- Use the debugger's Memory window to look at address `0x10` and read what it reports.

cards.q: How many bytes is a page on x64 Windows, and how many bits of an address are the offset within it?
cards.a:
4,096 bytes; the low 12 bits

2 to the power of 12 is 4,096, so 12 bits are needed to pick a byte within a page. 64 KB is the allocation granularity, not the page size.

One whose bits 48 to 63 all copy bit 47

Only canonical addresses are valid, which is why user-mode pointers on x64 start with `0000`. User-mode addresses are in the lower half, kernel ones in the upper half.

cards.q: What happens when a program touches a page that was paged out to disk?
cards.a:
A page fault: the kernel reads it back and resumes the program

The program only notices a delay; to it the memory was always there.

cards.q: What does the MMU replace when it translates an address?
cards.a:
The page number, with a physical frame number

Translation works page by page.

cards.q: Why does every user-mode pointer on x64 Windows start with `0000`?
cards.a:
User addresses are low, so the top 16 bits are zero

Canonical user-mode addresses have bits 48 to 63 equal to bit 47, which is 0.

cards.q: What is a demand-zero page fault?
cards.a:
A first touch of committed memory, given a zeroed page

It is invisible to the program, apart from a tiny delay.

cards.q: Why are page tables a tree rather than one flat array?
cards.a:
So only the parts of the address space in use need tables

A flat table for 48-bit addresses would need billions of entries per process.
